# THE "WORM THAT NEVER DIES."

For centuries, the cross stood for Christ and was addressed as if it were a living being. It was made divine at first and finally humanized.*

Few world-symbols are more filled with real occult meaning than the <term>Swastika</term> <note>original: "Svastika"</note>. It is symbolized by the number 6. Like that figure, its physical imagery points—just as the symbol for the number does—to the highest point (Zenith) and the lowest point (Nadir), as well as to the North, South, West, and East. One finds the "unit" everywhere, and that unit is reflected in each and every other unit. It is the emblem of the activity of <term>Fohat</term> <note>original: "Fohat"; in this context, the cosmic energy or "vital electricity" that drives the universe</note>, the continual revolution of the "Wheels" of existence, and the Four Elements—the "Sacred Four"—in their mystical and not just their physical sense. Furthermore, its four arms, bent at right angles, are intimately related, as shown elsewhere, to the scales used in Pythagorean and Hermetic philosophy. One initiated into the mysteries of the meaning of the <term>Swastika</term>, say the ancient *Commentaries*, "can trace on it, with mathematical precision, the evolution of the Cosmos and the entire period of <term>Sandhyâ</term> <note>original: "Sandhyâ"; the periods of twilight or transition between cosmic ages</note>." It also shows "the relation of the Seen to the Unseen" and "the first creation of humanity and all species."

To the Eastern occultist, the Tree of Knowledge—located in the paradise of a person's own heart—becomes the Tree of Eternal Life and has nothing to do with a person's animal senses. It is an absolute mystery that reveals itself only through the efforts of the imprisoned <term>Manas</term> <note>original: "Manas"; the mind or the human soul in Hindu philosophy</note>, the Ego, to liberate itself from the slavery of sensory perception and see by the light of the one eternal reality of the present. To the Western <term>Kabbalist</term> <note>original: "Kabalist"; a student of Jewish mysticism</note>, and even more so today to the superficial researcher of symbols who is raised in the suffocating atmosphere of materialistic science, the primary explanation for the mysteries of the cross is its sexual element. Even modern commentators who are otherwise spiritually minded notice this reproductive feature in the cross and <term>Swastika</term> before any others.

The cross was used in Egypt as a protecting talisman and a symbol of saving power. Typhon (or Satan) is actually found chained to and bound by the cross. In the *Ritual* <note>The Egyptian Book of the Dead</note>, the follower of Osiris cries, "*The <term>Apophis</term> is overthrown; their cords bind the South, North, East, and West; their cords are upon him. <term>Har-ru-bah</term> has knotted him.*"† These were the "Cords of the four quarters," or the cross. The god Thor is said to strike the head of the serpent with his hammer—a form of the <term>Swastika</term> or four-armed cross. In the primitive tombs of Egypt, the model of the Chamber—

## SECTION 11.
### THE MYSTERIES OF THE SEVEN. <note>original: "HEBDOMAD"</note>
---

We must not close this part on the symbolism of ancient history without attempting to explain the constant recurrence of this truly mystical number, the Seven <note>original: "Hebdomad"</note>, in every scripture known to scholars of Eastern cultures <note>original: "Orientalists"</note>. As every religion, from the oldest to the latest, reveals its presence and explains it on its own grounds in accordance with its own special doctrines, this is no easy task. We can, therefore, do no better or more explanatory work than to provide a bird’s-eye view of them all. The numbers 3, 4, and 7 are the sacred numbers of Light, Life, and Union—especially in this present <term>Manvantara</term> <note>a "Manvantara" is a vast period of time or "Life-Cycle" in Hindu cosmology</note>; of which number *seven* is the special representative or the governing factor. This must now be demonstrated.

If one should ask a <term>Brahman</term> learned in the <term>Upanishads</term> <note>ancient Sanskrit texts containing the philosophical core of Hinduism</note>, which are so full of the Secret Wisdom of old, why “he, of whom seven forefathers have drunk the juice of the Soma plant <note>original: "Moon-plant"</note>,” is called a <term>Trisuparna</term> <note>Sanskrit: "Three-winged" or "Three-leaved," referring to someone who has mastered specific sacred texts</note>, as the scholar <term>Bopaveda</term> is credited with saying;* and why the <term>Somapa Pitris</term> <note>Sanskrit: "Soma-drinking ancestors"</note> should be worshipped by the <term>Brahman Trisuparna</term>—very few could answer the question. Even if they knew, they would be even less likely to satisfy one's curiosity. Let us, then, hold to what the ancient Secret Doctrine <note>original: "Esoteric Doctrine"</note> teaches. As the Commentary says:

> When the first Seven appeared on Earth, they threw the seed of everything that grows on the land into the soil. *First came Three, and Four were added to these as soon as stone was transformed into plant. Then came the second Seven, who, guiding the life-essences <note>original: "Jîvas"</note> of the plants, produced the intermediate natures between plants and moving, living animals. The third Seven evolved their astral shadows <note>original: "Chhâyâs"</note>. . . . The fifth Seven imprisoned their Essence. . . . Thus man became a seven-leaved being <note>original: "Saptaparna"; a term for a seven-fold constitution, often symbolized by a seven-leaved plant</note>.*

* *Vishnu Purâna*, Wilson’s Translation, volume 3, page 174, note by Fitzedward Hall.

<header>THE "SYMBOLIC SIX-FOLD SIGN." <note>original: "HIEROGLYPHICAL SENARY"</note></header>

### A.
## SAPTAPARNA.

This is the name given to humanity in occult terminology. As shown elsewhere, it means a "seven-leaved plant," and the name carries great significance in Buddhist legends. It also appeared, though in disguise, in Greek myths. The T, or ⊤ (Tau), formed from the number 7 and the Greek letter Γ (Gamma), was—as stated in the previous section—the symbol of life and of Eternal Life. It represented earthly life because Γ (Gamma) is the symbol of the Earth (Gaia)*; and it represented Eternal Life because the number 7 is the symbol of that same life *linked* with Divine Life. This double symbol <term>glyph</term> <note>a symbolic figure or character</note> is expressed in geometrical figures as:

<image-desc>A geometric diagram consisting of a triangle placed directly on top of a square.</image-desc>
->△<-
->□<-

—a Triangle and a Square <note>original: "Quaternary"</note>, which is the symbol of Septenary <note>seven-fold</note> Man.

Now, in the Ancient Mysteries, the number *six* was regarded as an emblem of *physical* Nature. This is because six represents the six dimensions of all physical bodies—the *six* directions that create their form: namely, the four directions pointing to the cardinal points (North, South, East, and West), and the two directions of height and thickness that correspond to the Zenith <note>the point directly above</note> and the Nadir <note>the point directly below</note>. Therefore, while the Sages applied the Senary <note>the number six</note> to *physical* man, the Septenary <note>the number seven</note> was for them the symbol of that man *plus* his immortal Soul.†

J. M. Ragon gives an excellent illustration of what he calls the "hieroglyphical senary" <note>the symbolic six-fold sign</note>, which refers to our double equilateral triangle <note>the six-pointed star</note>.

> The symbolic six-fold sign is the symbol of the mixing of the *three philosophical fires* and *three waters*, from which results the creation of the elements of all things.‡

The same idea is found in the Indian double equilateral triangle. Although it is called the "Sign of Vishnu" in that country, it is actually the symbol of the Triad, or Tri-mûrti <note>the Hindu trinity of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva</note>. Even in the popular <note>original: "exoteric"</note> interpretation, the lower triangle (▽) with the point downward is the symbol of Vishnu, the God of the "Moist Principle" and Water. This is because Nârâyana <note>a name for Vishnu</note> is the Moving Principle in the Nârâ, or Waters.§ Meanwhile, the—

# THE SECRET DOCTRINE.

The triangle, with its apex upward, <image-desc>equilateral triangle with apex upward</image-desc>, is Shiva, the Principle of Fire, symbolized by the triple flame in his hand.* It is these two interlaced triangles—often incorrectly called "Solomon’s Seal," and which also form the emblem of our Society—that produce the Septenary <note>a group of seven</note> and the Triad <note>a group of three</note> at one and the same time, and together they represent the Decad <note>the number ten</note>. In whatever way this <image-desc>six-pointed star composed of two interlaced triangles</image-desc> is examined, all the ten numbers are contained within it. For with a point in the middle or center, <image-desc>six-pointed star with a central point</image-desc>, it is a sevenfold sign or Septenary; its triangles denote the number three, or the Triad; the two triangles show the presence of the Binary <note>the number two</note>; the triangles with the central point common to both yield the Quaternary <note>the number four</note>; the six points are the Senary <note>the number six</note>; and the central point is the Unit. The Quinary <note>the number five</note> is traced by combination, as a compound of *two* triangles (the even number) and *three* sides in each triangle (the first odd number). This is the reason why Pythagoras and the ancients made the number *six* sacred to Venus, since:

> The union of the two sexes, and the alchemical refinement <term>original: "spagyrization"</term> of matter by groups of three, are necessary to develop the generative force—that prolific power and tendency toward reproduction which is inherent in all bodies.†

Belief in "Creators," or the personified Powers of Nature, is in truth not polytheism but a philosophical necessity. Like all the other planets of our system, the Earth has seven Logoi <note>divine words or creative principles</note>—the emanating Rays of the one "Father-Ray"—the Protogonos <note>Greek for "First-born"</note>, or the Manifested Logos. He is the one who sacrifices his Being <note>original Latin: "Esse"</note> (or "Flesh," meaning the Universe) so that the World may live and every creature within it may have conscious existence.

Numbers 3 and 4 are respectively male and female, Spirit and Matter. Their union is the emblem of Eternal Life: in Spirit on its ascending arc, and in Matter as the ever-resurrecting Element through procreation and reproduction. The spiritual male line is vertical <image-desc>vertical line</image-desc>; the differentiated matter-line is horizontal; the two together form the cross, or <image-desc>cross symbol</image-desc>. The number 3 is invisible; the number 4 exists on the plane of objective perception. This is why all the matter of the Universe, when analyzed to its basic components by Science, can be reduced to only four Elements—Carbon, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and Hydrogen. It is also why the three primaries—the spiritual causes <term>noumena</term> <note>the intellectual or spiritual realities behind physical objects</note> of the four, or graduated Spirit or Force—have remained an unknown territory <note>original Latin: "terra incognita"</note> and mere speculation to exact Science. # THE THEOGONIC KEY.

The fundamental shape in *perceivable* <note>original: "manifested"</note> Nature is a square or a cube, represented by the numbers four and six. As William Enfield <note>William Enfield (1741–1797) was a British author known for his "History of Philosophy."</note> says, "since the particles of earth are cubical, those of fire are pyramidal"—and this is quite true. The pyramid shape is the same one taken by pine trees, which were the most primitive trees to appear after the age of ferns. In this way, the two opposites in cosmic Nature—fire and water, heat and cold—begin their geometric <note>original: "metrographical"</note> expressions: one through a three-sided <note>original: "trimetric"</note> system and the other through a six-sided <note>original: "hexagonal"</note> system. For instance, snow crystals—which look like stars under a microscope—are all double or triple six-pointed stars, each containing a tiny central star inside the larger one. 

Charles Darwin also shows that creatures living on the sea-shore are deeply affected by the tides:

> The most ancient ancestors in the vertebrate kingdom <note>original: "Vertebrata"</note>... apparently consisted of a group of marine animals... Animals living near either the *average* high-water mark or the *average* low-water mark experience a complete cycle of tidal changes every fortnight [two weeks]... Now, it is a mysterious fact that in the higher, land-based vertebrates... many healthy and diseased processes have cycles of one or more weeks [seven-day periods <term>septenates</term>]... such as the pregnancy <note>original: "gestation"</note> of mammals and the duration of fevers.*

The eggs of the pigeon hatch in two weeks (14 days); those of the chicken in three; those of the duck in four; those of the goose in five; and those of the ostrich in seven.†

This number seven is closely connected with the Moon, whose hidden <note>original: "Occult"</note> influence is always revealing itself in seven-day periods. The Moon is the guide for the hidden side of nature on Earth, while the Sun is the regulator and creator of visible life. This truth has always been obvious to visionaries and spiritual masters. Jakob Böhme <note>Jakob Böhme (1575–1624) was a German Christian mystic who influenced later Western esotericism.</note>, by insisting on the fundamental doctrine of the "seven properties of everlasting Mother Nature," proved himself to be a great student of hidden wisdom <note>original: "Occultist"</note>.

This explains the verses of *Genesis*: “Of every clean beast you shall take to you by sevens, the male [3], and the female [4]; of birds also of the air by sevens,”† etc., followed by all the other *sevening* of days and the rest.

## B.

### THE TETRAKTYS IN RELATION TO THE HEPTAGON.

Thus the number *seven*, as a compound of 3 and 4, is the primary element in every ancient religion because it is the *primary element in Nature*. Its adoption must be justified, and it must be shown to be the number *par excellence* <note>the best or most essential example</note>. Since the publication of *Esoteric Buddhism* <note>An 1883 book by A.P. Sinnett that introduced these concepts to the West</note>, frequent objections have been made and doubts expressed regarding the correctness of these assertions.

At this point, the student should be told immediately that in all such numerical divisions, the One Universal Principle—although referred to as "the One" because it is the Only One—never enters into the calculations. In its character as the Absolute, the Infinite, and the Universal Abstraction, it stands entirely by itself and is independent of every other power, whether spiritual <note>original: "noumenal"</note> or physical <note>original: "phenomenal"</note>. As the author of the article “Personal and Impersonal God” says:

This entity is neither matter nor spirit; it is neither the Self <note>original: "Ego"</note> nor the not-self <note>original: "non-Ego"</note>; and it is neither object nor subject.

In the language of Hindu philosophers, it is the original and eternal combination of *Purusha* <note>Spirit</note> and *Prakriti* <note>Matter</note>. As the Advaita Vedantists <note>original: "Advaitîs"; followers of the school of Hindu philosophy that emphasizes the oneness of the individual soul and the Supreme Reality</note> hold that an external object is merely the product of our mental states, *Prakriti* <note>Matter or Nature</note> is nothing more than illusion, and *Purusha* <note>Spirit</note> is the only reality; it is the *one* existence which remains in the universe of Ideas. This, then, is the <term>Parabrahman</term> <note>the Supreme Absolute or the "Boundless"</note> of the Advaita Vedantists. Even if there were a personal God with something like a material <term>Upadhi</term> <note>Sanskrit: "basis" or "limiting condition"; a physical vehicle or form</note>, from the standpoint of an Advaita Vedantist, there would be as much reason to doubt his essential existence <note>original: "noumenal existence"</note> as there would be for any other object. In their opinion, a conscious God cannot be the origin of the universe, as his sense of "I" <note>original: "Ego"</note> would be the effect of a previous cause, if the word conscious carries only its ordinary meaning. They cannot admit that the *grand total of all the states of consciousness in the universe* is their deity, as these states are constantly changing, and because cosmic idealism ceases during <term>Pralaya</term> <note>Sanskrit: a period of cosmic rest or dissolution where the universe is not manifested</note>. There is only one permanent condition in the Universe: the state of perfect unconsciousness, which is actually bare <term>Chidakasha</term> <note>original: *Chidâkâsham*; the infinite field or "sky" of pure consciousness</note>.

<margin>* *Five Years of Theosophy*, pages 202, 203.</margin>
Once my readers realize the fact that this grand universe is in reality only a huge collection of various states of consciousness, they will not be surprised to find that the ultimate state of unconsciousness is considered the Supreme Absolute <note>original: "Parabrahman"</note> by the Advaita Vedantists.*

<margin>† Ibid., page 200.</margin>
Although it is entirely beyond human reckoning or calculation, this “huge collection of various states of consciousness” is a sevenfold system <note>original: "septenate"</note>. In *its totality*, it is composed entirely of groups of seven—simply because “the capacity for perception exists in seven different aspects corresponding to the seven conditions of matter,”† or the seven properties or states of matter. Therefore, in *Esoteric* <note>inner-circle or secret</note> calculations, the series from one to seven begins with the first manifested principle. This is number one if we count from above, and number seven when reckoning from below, or from the lowest principle.

The <term>Tetrad</term> <note>the number four</note> is held in high regard in the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note>, as it was by Pythagoras, as the most perfect or *sacred* number. This is because it flowed <note>original: "emanated"</note> from the One—the first manifested Unit, or rather the Three-in-One. This latter concept has always been impersonal, sexless, and incomprehensible, though it is within the reach of the higher mental perceptions.

The first manifestation of the eternal Monad <note>the ultimate, indivisible Unity</note> was never intended to represent another symbol—the Unborn for the Element-born, or the one Logos <note>Divine Word or Reason</note> for the Heavenly Man. The <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>Greek: "four letters"; the sacred four-letter name of God</note>, or the <term>Tetraktys</term> <note>a triangular figure of ten points used by the Pythagoreans</note> of the Greeks, is the Second Logos, the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>original: *Demiurgos*; the creator or fashioner of the material world</note>.

The Tetrad, as the scholar Thomas Taylor thinks, is, however, the “Self-Animal” <note>original: *animal itself*; a reference to Plato's *Autozoon*, the ideal living creature or world-soul</note> of Plato. Plato, as Syrianus <note>a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> rightly observes, was the best of the Pythagoreans. ...third book of his treatise on the theology of Plato. And between these two triads [the double triangle], the one being intelligible <note>original: "intelligible," meaning perceptible by the mind rather than the senses</note> and the other being intellectual, another order of gods exists that partakes of both extremes.* . . .

*The Pythagorean world, according to Plutarch,† consisted of a double quaternary <note>original: "quaternary," a set of four</note>.*

This statement corroborates what is said about the choice, by public <note>original: "exoteric"</note> theologies, of the *lower <term>Tetraktys</term>* <note>the sacred Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle, here referring specifically to the number four</note>. For:

The quaternary of the intellectual world [the world of *Mahat*, or Divine Mind] consists of *T'Agathon* <note>original: "T’Agathon," Greek for "The Good"</note>, *Nous* <note>original: "Nous," Greek for "Mind"</note>, *Psyche* <note>original: "Psyche," Greek for "Soul"</note>, and *Hyle* <note>original: "Hyle," Greek for "Matter"</note>; while that of the sensible world [of Matter], which is properly what Pythagoras meant by the word *Kosmos*, consists of Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. These four elements are called by the name of <term>rhizômata</term> <note>Greek for "roots"</note>, the roots or principles of all mixed bodies.‡

That is to say, the lower Tetraktys is the root of illusion—of the World of Matter. This is the *Tetragrammaton* <note>the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note> of the Jews, and the "mysterious deity" over which modern Kabbalists make such a fuss!

This number [*four*] forms the arithmetical middle point <note>original: "mean"</note> between the one <note>original: "monad"</note> and the seven <note>original: "heptad"</note>. It encompasses all powers, both of the numbers that produce and those that are produced. Of all numbers under ten, this one is made of a certain number: two <note>original: "duad"</note> doubled makes a four <note>original: "tetrad"</note>, and the four doubled [or unfolded] makes the seven <note>original: "hebdomad" or "septenary"</note>. Two multiplied by itself produces four; and when cubed <note>original: "retorted into itself"</note>, it makes the first cube. *This first cube is a fertile number, the foundation of multitude and variety, consisting of two and four [depending on the one, or the seventh].* Thus the two principles of temporary things—the pyramid <note>original: "pyramis"</note> and the cube, representing form and matter—flow from one fountain: the four-sided figure <note>original: "tetragon"</note> [on earth, the one, in heaven].§

Here Reuchlin, the great authority on the *Kabalah*, shows the cube to represent "matter," whereas the pyramid or the three <note>original: "triad"</note> represents "form." According to the followers of Hermes <note>original: "Hermesians"</note>, the number four becomes the symbol of truth only when expanded into a cube. When unfolded, this cube makes seven, symbolizing the male and female elements and the element of Life.||

-># THE “VOICE OF NATURE.”<-

Some students have been puzzled to explain why the vertical line (which is male) becomes a four-part line in the cross—four being a female number—while the horizontal line (the line of matter) becomes three-parted. But this is easy to explain. Since the middle square <note>original: "face"</note> of the “unfolded cube” is shared <note>original: "common"</note> by both the vertical and the horizontal bars, it becomes neutral ground, so to speak, and belongs to neither. Therefore, the spirit line remains a group of three <note>original: "triadic"</note>, and the matter line remains twofold—two being an even and therefore also a female number. Furthermore, according to Theon in his *Mathematical Matters* <note>original: *Mathematica*</note>, the Pythagoreans (who gave the name “Harmony” to the <term>Tetraktys</term> <note>the sacred Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle</note> because it represents a perfect fourth in a 4:3 ratio <note>original: "diatessaron in sesquitertia"</note>) were of the opinion that:

> The division of the scale <note>original: "canon"</note> of the monochord <note>a one-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note> was created by the Tetraktys through the numbers two, three, and four. For it contains ratios of 4:3, 3:2, 2:1, 3:1, and 4:1 <note>original: "sesquitertia, a sesquialtera, a duple, a triple, and a quadruple proportion"</note>, the sum <note>original: "section"</note> of which is 27. In ancient musical notation, the <term>tetrachord</term> <note>a series of four notes</note> consisted of three steps or intervals and four musical notes <note>original: "terms of sounds"</note>, called by the Greeks a *diatessaron* and by us a fourth.*

Additionally, the number four <note>original: "quaternary"</note>, though it is an even and therefore female (or underworld <note>original: "infernal"</note>) number, changed its meaning according to its form. This is shown by Thomas Stanley.† The four was called by the Pythagoreans the “Key-Keeper of Nature.” However, when joined with the three (making seven), it became the most perfect and harmonious number—nature herself. The four was described as "the masculine of feminine form" when it formed the cross. Furthermore, seven is the “Master of the Moon,” because that planet is forced to change its appearance every seven days. It is upon the number seven that Pythagoras built his doctrine of the Harmony and Music of the Spheres. He defined a “tone” as the distance from the Moon to the Earth; from the Moon to Mercury was half a tone, and the same from Mercury to Venus; from Venus to the Sun was one and a half tones; from the Sun to Mars was one tone; from Mars to Jupiter was half a tone; from Jupiter to Saturn was half a tone; and from Saturn to the Zodiac was one tone. This created a total of seven tones—the complete scale <note>original: "diapason harmony"</note>.‡ All the melody of Nature exists within those seven tones, and it is therefore called the “Voice of Nature.”

Plutarch explains§ that the most ancient Greeks regarded the <term>Tetrad</term> <note>the number four</note> as the root and principle of all things, since it was the number of the elements that gave birth to all visible and invisible created things.||

Among the members of the Rosicrucian Order <note>original: "brothers of the Rosy Cross"</note>, the image of the cross—or the *unfolded cube*—was the topic of a formal discussion in one of the Theosophical degrees of Peuvret <note>Jean-Pierre Peuvret was a French occultist known for his esoteric degrees</note>. This symbol was analyzed based on the core principles of light and darkness, *or good and evil.*\*

The world of pure intellect <note>original: "intelligible world"</note> emerges from the divine mind [or the Unit] in the following way. The <term>Tetraktys</term> <note>a sacred Pythagorean symbol of ten points arranged in a triangle</note>, reflecting upon its own essence—the *first unit, the producer of all things*—and upon its own beginning, says this: "One times one, two times two," and immediately a <term>tetrad</term> <note>a group of four</note> arises. This tetrad has the highest unit at its peak and *becomes a pyramid*, with a base that is a flat square <note>original: "plain tetrad"</note> representing a surface. Upon this surface, the radiant light of the divine unity creates the *form of bodiless fire* <note>original: "incorporeal fire"</note>, caused by the descent of Juno (representing matter) into lower realms. From this comes essential light, which does not burn but illuminates. This is the *creation of the middle world*, which the Hebrews call the *Supreme*, the world of their deity. It is called Olympus—completely light and filled with distinct forms—which is the seat of the immortal gods, *the high home of the gods* <note>original: "deûm domus alta"</note>. *Its peak is unity, its wall is trinity, and its surface is quaternity.*†

The "surface" <note>original: "superficies"</note> remains a *meaningless plane* if left alone. Since Unity only "illuminates" the *quaternity* <note>the group of four</note>, the famous "lower four" must also build a wall for itself out of the *trinity* if it is to become manifest. Furthermore, the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note>, or <term>Microprosopus</term> <note>the "Lesser Face" in Kabbalistic tradition, representing the manifested God</note>, is "Jehovah"—falsely claiming for himself the title "Was, Is, and Will Be" (now translated as "I am that I am"). This is often interpreted as referring to the highest abstract Deity. However, *esoterically* and in plain truth, it represents only the periodically chaotic, turbulent, and eternal Matter, along with all its potential. For the Tetragrammaton is one with Nature, or Isis, and represents the outer <note>original: "exoteric"</note> series of <term>androgynous</term> <note>having both male and female characteristics</note> gods, such as Osiris-Isis, Jove-Juno, Brahma-Vach, or the Kabalistic Jah-Hovah; they are all male-female pairs. As Marsilio Ficino <note>original: "Marcellus Ficin," a 15th-century Italian philosopher</note> correctly noted, every human-like god among ancient nations had a name written with four letters. For the Egyptians, it was Teut; for the Arabs, Alla; for the Persians, Sire; for the Magi, Orsi; for the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, Abdi; for the Greeks, Teos; for the ancient Turks, Esar; for the Latins, Deus; to which Giovanni Lorenzo Anania adds the German Gott, the Slavic <note>original: "Sarmatian"</note> Bouh, and so on.‡

Because the <term>Monad</term> <note>the number one, representing unity and the source of all numbers</note> is one and an odd number, the ancients claimed that odd numbers were the only perfect ones. They considered them all masculine and perfect—perhaps a selfish view, but a factual one in their system—and applied them to the heavenly gods. In contrast, even numbers like two, four, six, and especially eight were seen as female and regarded as imperfect; these were assigned only to the gods of the earth and the underworld <note>original: "infernal Deities"</note>. # THE SEPTENARY DEMONSTRATED.

...the fact by saying, "God delights in an odd number" <note>original Latin: "Numero deus impare gaudet"</note>.*

But the number **seven**, or the <term>Heptad</term> <note>the number seven or a group of seven</note>, was considered by the followers of Pythagoras to be a **religious and perfect number**. It was called <term>Telesphoros</term> <note>Greek for "bringing to an end" or "perfection"</note> because, through it, everything in the universe and humanity is led to **its end**—meaning its highest point or culmination.† The doctrine of the "Spheres" ruled by the seven Sacred Planets‡ shows, from the time of <term>Lemuria</term> <note>a hypothetical lost continent in ancient esoteric history</note> to the time of Pythagoras, the seven powers of earthly and <term>sublunary</term> <note>literally "below the moon," meaning the physical world</note> Nature. It also shows the seven great forces of the universe, which proceed and evolve in seven tones—the seven notes of the musical scale.

The Heptad (our <term>Septenary</term> <note>a set or system based on the number seven</note>) was considered the **number of a virgin because it is unborn**. In this sense, it is like the <term>Logos</term> <note>the divine word or creative principle</note> or the *Aja* <note>Sanskrit for "unborn"</note> of the Vedantic philosophers:

*It is without a father or a mother, but proceeds directly from the unit <note>original: "monad"</note>, which is the origin and crown of all things.*§

And if the Heptad is said to proceed directly from the divine unit, then it is—as taught in the Secret Doctrine of the oldest schools—the perfect and sacred number of our current <term>Mahamanvantara</term> <note>in Hindu cosmology, a vast period of time during which a universe exists</note>.

The Septenary, or Heptad, was indeed sacred to several gods and goddesses: to Mars, with his seven attendants; to Osiris, whose body was divided into seven and twice seven parts; to Apollo, the Sun, surrounded by his seven planets and playing a hymn to the "seven-rayed" on his seven-stringed harp; to Minerva, who was fatherless and motherless; and to others.||

<term>Cis-Himalayan</term> <note>literally "on this side of the Himalayas," referring to a specific lineage of esoteric knowledge</note> Occultism, with its focus on "sevening" (organizing by sevens), must be regarded as the most ancient and the original of all because of this structure. This view is opposed by some fragments left by the Neo-Platonists. The admirers of the Neo-Platonists—who hardly understand what they are defending—say to us: "See, your predecessors believed only in a triple nature of man, composed of Spirit, Soul, and Body." They point out that the <term>Taraka Raja Yoga</term> <note>a system of yoga focusing on spiritual liberation</note> of India limits that division to 3, we limit it to 4, and the <term>Vedantins</term> <note>followers of the Vedanta school of Indian philosophy</note> limit it to 5 <term>Koshas</term> <note>Sanskrit for "sheaths" or layers covering the soul</note>. To this, we of the Ancient <note>original: "Archaic"</note> school ask:

Why then does the Greek poet say that it is not four, but **seven** who sing the praise of the Spiritual Sun?

# THE SEVENFOLD ELEMENT IN THE VEDAS.
## IT SUPPORTS THE SECRET TEACHING CONCERNING THE SEVEN GLOBES AND THE SEVEN RACES.

We must return to the very source of historical information if we wish to present our best evidence for these facts. In these hymns, the seven rays of **Sûrya** <note>the Sun god</note> are equated with the seven worlds of every planetary chain, and with the seven rivers of heaven and earth—the former representing the seven creative hosts and the latter representing the seven men, or primitive human groups. The seven ancient **Rishis** <note>inspired sages or seers</note>—the ancestors of all that lives and breathes on Earth—are the seven friends of **Agni** <note>the god of fire</note>, his seven "**horses,**" or seven "**heads.**" It is allegorically stated that the human race sprang from fire and water, fashioned from Agni by the "Fathers" or "Ancestor-Sacrificers." For Agni, the **Ashvins** <note>divine twin horsemen</note>, and the **Âdityas**† <note>solar deities</note> are all synonymous with those "Sacrificers" or "Fathers," who are variously called **Pitris** (ancestors), **Angirasas**,‡ and **Sâdhyas**—the "**Divine Sacrificers,**" who are the most hidden <note>original: Occult</note> of all. Yima—the so-called "first man" in the *Vendidad* <note>a collection of texts within the larger Zoroastrian Avesta</note>—belongs to two epochs of universal history, much like his twin brother Yama (the son of Vaivasvata Manu). He is the ancestor <note>original: "Progenitor"</note> of the Second human Race; therefore, he is the personification of the "Shadows" of the Pitris <note>the lunar ancestors or spirits of the forefathers</note> and the Father of humanity after the Great Flood <note>original: "Postdiluvian Humanity"</note>. The Magi <note>ancient Persian priests</note> said "Yima" the same way we say "man" when speaking of mankind. The "fair Yima," the first mortal who speaks with Ahura Mazda <note>the supreme god of Zoroastrianism</note>, is the *first "man" who dies or disappears*, not the first who is born. The "son of Vivanghat" was, like the son of Vaivasvata, the symbolic man who represented the *first three Races* and their collective ancestor within the Secret Doctrine <note>original: "Esotericism"</note>. Of these Races, the first two never died but only vanished, being absorbed into their own offspring. The Third Race only experienced death toward its end, after the separation of the sexes and its "Fall" into physical reproduction. This is clearly mentioned in the second chapter <note>original: "Fargard ii"</note> of the *Vendidad*. Yima refuses to become the messenger of the law of Ahura Mazda, saying:

<margin>‡ In the work previously cited, p. 12.</margin>
> "I was not born, I was not taught to be the preacher and the bearer of your law."‡

And then Ahura Mazda asks him to make his men multiply and to "watch over" his world.

Yima refuses to become the priest of Ahura Mazda because he is *his own priest and sacrificer*, but he accepts the second proposal. He is recorded as answering:

> "Yes! . . . Yes, I will nourish, and rule, and watch over your world. There shall be, while I am king, neither cold wind nor hot wind, *neither disease nor death*."

Then Ahura Mazda brings him a golden ring and a dagger <note>original: "poniard"</note>, the emblems of sovereignty.

Thus, under the rule of Yima, three hundred *winters* passed away, and the earth was replenished with flocks and herds, with men and dogs and birds, and with red blazing fires.

# THE "BREATHS" OF THE "ONE BREATH."

Pay close attention to the word "replenished"; this implies that everything had existed on the Earth previously. This proves that there was ancient knowledge regarding the doctrine of the successive destructions of the world and its cycles of life. Once the "three hundred winters" were over, <term>Ahura Mazda</term> <note>the supreme creator god of Zoroastrianism</note> warns <term>Yima</term> <note>a mythological king and the first man in Zoroastrian tradition</note> that the Earth is becoming too crowded and the people have nowhere to live. Then <term>Yima</term> steps forward and, with the help of <term>Spenta Armaita</term> <note>the female spirit or guardian of the Earth</note>, causes the Earth to stretch out and expand by one-third. Afterward, "new flocks, herds, and people" appear upon it. <term>Ahura Mazda</term> warns him again, and <term>Yima</term> uses the same magical power to make the Earth grow by two-thirds. After "nine hundred winters" pass, <term>Yima</term> must perform the ceremony for the *third* time.

This entire account is allegorical. The three processes of stretching the Earth refer to the three successive continents and human races that emerged one after another, as explained more fully in other sections of this work. After the *third* expansion, <term>Ahura Mazda</term> warns <term>Yima</term> during an assembly of "celestial gods" and "excellent mortals" that deadly winters are about to descend upon the material world, and all *life* will perish. This is the ancient Mazdean <note>Zoroastrian</note> symbolism for the "Flood" and the coming cataclysm to <term>Atlantis</term> <note>a legendary lost continent often cited in occult history</note>, which sweeps away every race in its turn. Like <term>Vaivasvata Manu</term> <note>the Hindu equivalent of Noah</note> and <term>Noah</term>, <term>Yima</term> builds a <term>Vara</term>—an enclosure or ark—under the God's direction. He brings into it the seeds of every living creature, including animals and "Fires" <note>likely referring to spiritual or essential energies</note>.

It was on this "Earth" or new continent that <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>original: "Zarathushtra"</note> became the lawgiver and ruler. This marked the beginning of the <term>Fourth Race</term>, occurring after the people of the <term>Third Race</term> began to die out. Until then, as mentioned previously, there was no regular death—only a transformation—because *humans did not yet possess a personal identity*. They possessed <term>Monads</term> <note>indivisible units of spirit or consciousness</note>—which were "Breaths" of the <term>One Breath</term>, as impersonal as the source from which they originated. They had bodies, or rather "shadows" of bodies, which were sinless and therefore free from the law of cause and effect <note>original: "Karma-less"</note>. 

Because there was no <term>Kama Loka</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "desire world"; an intermediate state after death</note>—and certainly no <term>Nirvana</term> <note>spiritual liberation</note> or even <term>Devachan</term> <note>a peaceful, heavenly state between lives</note>—for the souls of people who lacked personal <term>Egos</term>, there could be no intermediate periods between incarnations. Like the <term>Phoenix</term> <note>a mythical bird that is reborn from its own ashes</note>, primordial humanity was resurrected out of the old body into a new one. With each new generation, the human form became more solid and physically developed, in accordance with the law of evolution, which is the <term>Law of Nature</term>. Physical death only began once the physical organism was fully formed, and with it came moral decay.

This explanation shows yet another ancient religion whose symbolism agrees with the <term>Universal Doctrine</term> <note>the core set of spiritual truths the author argues underlies all religions</note>.

Elsewhere the oldest Persian traditions, the remains of Mazdeism <note>original: "Mazdeism"; the ancient religion of Zoroastrianism</note> from the still older Magians <note>original: "Magians"; ancient Persian priests and astronomers</note>, are presented and some of them explained. Mankind did not originate from one single couple. Nor was there ever a "first man"—whether Adam or Yima—but rather a first humanity.

It may, or may not, be "mitigated polygenism" <note>the theory that different human races evolved from several independent ancestors</note>. Once both creation *out of nothing* <note>original: "ex nihilo"</note> (an absurdity) and a superhuman Creator or Creators (a fact) are dismissed by Science, polygenism presents no more difficulties or inconveniences—and perhaps fewer from a scientific perspective—than monogenism <note>the theory that all humans descend from a single pair</note> does.

In fact, it is as scientific as any other claim. For in his introduction to Nott and Gliddon’s *Types of Mankind*, Agassiz <note>Louis Agassiz (1807–1873), a famous Swiss-American biologist and geologist</note> declares his belief in an unlimited number of "original races of men created *separately*"; and remarks that, "while in every animal region <note>original: "zoological province"</note> animals belong to *different* species, man, despite the diversity of his races, always forms *one and the same* human being."

<margin>Irenæus, Book I. xxiv. 1.</margin>
Occultism <note>the study of hidden spiritual knowledge</note> defines and limits the number of original races to seven, because of the seven "Progenitors" <note>ancestors</note>, or <term>Prajâpatis</term> <note>in Hindu tradition, the "Lords of Creatures" who assisted in creation</note>, the developers of all beings. These are neither gods nor supernatural beings, but advanced spirits from another and lower planet, reborn on this planet, and giving birth in their turn in the present "Round" <note>a major cycle of planetary evolution</note> to current humanity. This doctrine is again supported by one of its echoes among the Gnostics <note>an early mystical branch of Christianity</note>. In their study of human origins and genesis, they taught that "a certain company of *seven angels*" formed the first men, who were nothing more than mindless, giant, shadow-like forms—"a mere wriggling worm" (!) writes Irenæus <note>a 2nd-century Christian bishop and critic of Gnosticism</note>, who takes, as usual, the metaphor for literal reality.

3. A full jar is contained in Time. We behold him existing in many forms. He is all these worlds in the future. They call him "Time in the highest Heaven." §

# THE SECRET DOCTRINE.

Thus, from the seven Creations, seven Rishis <note>sages or seers</note>, Zones, Continents, Principles, and so on, in the Aryan Scriptures, the number has passed through Indian, Egyptian, Chaldean, Greek, Jewish, Roman, and finally Christian mystic thought, until it landed in, and remained permanently impressed on, every external <note>original: "exoteric"</note> theology. The seven old books stolen out of Noah’s Ark by Ham and given to his son Cush, and the seven Brazen Columns of Ham and Chiron, are a reflection and a memory of the seven primordial Mysteries established according to the "seven secret Emanations," the seven Sounds, and seven Rays—the spiritual and celestial <note>original: "sidereal"</note> models of the seven thousand times seven copies of them in later ages <note>original: "æons"</note>.

The mysterious number is once more prominent in the no less mysterious Maruts <note>storm deities in Hindu mythology</note>. The *Vâyu Purâna* shows, and the *Harivamsha* confirms, concerning the Maruts—the oldest as well as the most incomprehensible of all the secondary or lower Gods in the *Rig Veda*:

# WHO ARE THE MARUTS?

Diti, anxious to obtain a son who would destroy Indra, is told by the sage Kashyapa that if, "with thoughts wholly pious and person entirely pure," she carries the baby in her womb "for a hundred years,"* she will have such a son. But Indra ruins her plan. With his thunderbolt, *he divides the embryo in her womb into seven portions*, and then divides every such portion into *seven pieces again*, which become the swift-moving deities, the Maruts <note>storm deities in Hindu mythology</note>.† These deities are only another aspect, or a development, of the Kumâras <term>eternal virgin youths</term>, who are known as Rudras by their father's name, like many others.‡

Diti, being Aditi <note>the "Boundless," the mother of the gods</note>—unless the contrary is proven to us—Aditi, we say, or Âkâsha <term>spiritual ether or space</term> in her highest form, is the Egyptian *seven-fold Heaven*. Every true occultist will understand what this means. Diti, we repeat, is the sixth principle of *metaphysical Nature*, the Buddhi <note>the faculty of intuitive wisdom</note> of Âkâsha. Diti, the Mother of the Maruts, is one of her earthly forms, made to represent, at one and the same time, the Divine Soul in the ascetic and the divine aspirations of mystic humanity toward deliverance from the webs of Mâyâ <term>the illusion of the material world</term> and the resulting final bliss. 

Indra is now viewed as a lower figure because of the Kali Yuga <note>the current "Dark Age" of materialism and spiritual ignorance</note>, when such aspirations are no longer common but have become abnormal through a general spread of Ahamkâra—the feeling of egotism, or "I-am-ness"—and ignorance. But in the beginning, Indra was one of the greatest gods of the Hindu collection of deities, as the *Rig Veda* shows. Surâdhipa, the "chief of the gods," has fallen from being Jishnu, the "Leader of the Celestial Host"—the Hindu equivalent of Saint Michael—to being an opponent of asceticism and the enemy of every holy aspiration. He is shown married to Aindrî (Indrânî), the personification of Aindriyaka <note>the world of the senses</note>, whom he married "because of her sensual attractions." After this, he began sending celestial female demons to excite the passions of holy men and Yogis, "to lead them away from the powerful spiritual practices which he feared." Therefore, Indra—now characterized as "the god of the sky, the personified atmosphere"—is in reality the cosmic principle Mahat <term>Universal Mind</term> and the fifth human principle, Manas <term>individual mind</term> in its dual aspect: both as it is connected with Buddhi and as it allows itself to be dragged down by the Kâma <note>passion or desire</note> principle.

# THE DOOM OF CONTINUAL RE-BIRTH.

...reached it, they remain invisible on Earth. Therefore, the <term>Maruts</term> <note>Vedic storm deities associated here with spiritual forces</note> are shown, firstly, as the sons of <term>Shiva-Rudra</term>, the Patron <term>Yogi</term> <note>the divine master of meditation and asceticism</note>, whose Third Eye (mystically) must be acquired by the ascetic before he becomes an <term>Adept</term> <note>a master of spiritual and secret knowledge</note>. Then, in their cosmic character, they are shown as the subordinates of <term>Indra</term> and his opponents, appearing under various names. 

The twenty-eight <note>original: "four times seven"</note> emancipations refer to the four Rounds and the four Races that preceded ours. # THE SECRET DOCTRINE.

# THE CYCLE OF THE NAROS.

The sisters, the Pleiades, are necessary for the completion of this most secret and mysterious of all astronomical and religious symbols. Therefore, when intended to commemorate one particular event, Kârttikeya <note>The Hindu god of war and son of Shiva</note> was shown in ancient times as a *Kumâra* <note>original: "Kumâra"; a youthful ascetic or celibate boy</note>, an ascetic with *six* heads—one for each century of the Naros <term>Naros</term> <note>A cyclic period, often defined as 600 years, used in ancient calculations to synchronize solar and lunar time</note>. 

When the symbolism was needed for another event, Kârttikeya is seen in conjunction with the seven sidereal sisters and accompanied by Kaumârî (or Senâ), his female aspect. He is then riding on a peacock, the bird of wisdom and occult knowledge. This is the Hindu version of the Phoenix, and its Greek connection with the 600 years of the Naros is well known. A six-rayed star (a double triangle), a swastika, and a six-pointed (occasionally seven-pointed) crown sit on his brow. In India, the years of the Naros are counted in two ways: either by one hundred "years of the gods" (divine years) or one hundred "mortal years." Because of this, we can see the tremendous difficulty that uninitiated people have in reaching a correct understanding of this cycle. The eighth element in this list is, in a sense, the octave <note>In music, an octave is the eighth note that repeats the tone of the first at a higher pitch; here, it refers to elements repeating properties every eight steps</note> of the first, and the ninth is the octave of the second, and so on. Each element is almost identical in its properties to the corresponding element in each of the sevenfold <note>original: septenary</note> rows. This phenomenon emphasizes the sevenfold law of periodicity <note>The Law of Octaves, a precursor to the modern Periodic Law developed by Newlands and Mendeleev</note>. For further details, the reader is referred to the work of Hellenbach <note>Lazar Baron von Hellenbach, a 19th-century philosopher and scientist</note>, where it is also shown that this classification is confirmed by the unique patterns of light <note>original: spectroscopic peculiarities</note> emitted by the elements.

It is unnecessary to describe in detail the number of vibrations that make up the notes of the musical scale; they are exactly similar <note>original: strictly analogous</note> to the scale of chemical elements, and also to the scale of color as revealed by the spectroscope <note>An instrument used to measure the properties of light</note>. However, in the case of light, we deal with only *one* octave, while in both music and chemistry, we find a series of *seven* octaves represented theoretically. Of these, *six* are fairly complete and commonly used in both sciences. To quote Hellenbach:

> It has been established that, from the standpoint of the law of appearances <note>original: phenomenal law</note> upon which all our knowledge rests, the vibrations of sound and light increase regularly. They divide themselves into *seven* columns, and the successive numbers in each column are closely related. That is <note>original: i.e.</note>, they exhibit a close relationship that is not only expressed in the figures themselves but is also practically confirmed in chemistry and in music. In music, the ear confirms what the numbers show. . . . The fact that this periodicity and variety is governed by the number seven is undeniable. It goes far beyond the limits of mere chance and must be assumed to have an adequate cause, which must be discovered.

Truly, then, as Rabbi Abba said:

> We are six lights which shine forth from a seventh light; you, the Four-Letter Name of God <note>original: Tetragrammaton</note>, are the seventh light—the origin of us all. For certainly there is no stability in those six except for what they derive from the seventh. For all things depend on the seventh.*

<page-num>665</page-num>
<header>THE SEVEN PRIESTS OF THE ZUÑIS.</header>

The ancient and modern Zuñi Indians of Western America seem to have held similar views. Their present-day customs, traditions, and records all point to the fact that, from ancient times, their political, social, and religious institutions were, and still are, shaped according to the <term>septenary principle</term> <note>original: "septenary principle"; the rule or system based on the number seven</note>. For example, all their ancient towns and villages were built in clusters of six around a seventh. It is always a group of seven, or of thirteen, and the six always surround the seventh. Furthermore, their religious hierarchy is composed of six “Priests of the House,” who seem to be unified in the seventh, who is a woman, the “Priestess Mother.” Compare this with the “seven great officiating priests” mentioned in the *Anugita* <note>original: *Anugîtâ*; a Sanskrit philosophical text that is part of the Mahabharata</note>—the name given to the “seven senses” in public teachings, and to the seven human principles in spiritual <note>original: "Esoterically"</note> teachings. Why is this symbolism identical? Should we still doubt the story of Arjuna <note>A hero from the Hindu epic, the Mahabharata</note> traveling to the Underworld <note>original: *Pâtâla*; in Hindu mythology, the regions opposite the earth, often interpreted by the author as the Antipodes or America</note> and there marrying Ulupi, the daughter of the Serpent King <note>original: "Nâga, or rather Nargal, king"; Nâgas are semi-divine serpent beings in Hindu and Buddhist mythology</note>? But let us return to the Zuñi priests.

To this day, these priests receive an annual tribute of corn in seven colors. During most of the year, they are indistinguishable from other Indians, but on a certain day they appear—six priests and one priestess—dressed in their priestly robes. Each robe is a color sacred to the specific God whom the priest serves and represents; each priest represents one of the seven regions, and each receives corn of the color corresponding to that region. 

The colors are assigned as follows:
*   **White** represents the East, because the first sunlight comes from the East.
*   **Yellow** corresponds to the North, from the color of the flames produced by the Northern Lights <note>original: "Aurora Borealis"</note>.
*   **Red** represents the South, as heat comes from that direction.
*   **Blue** stands for the West, the color of the Pacific Ocean, which lies to the West.
*   **Black** is the color of the lower underground region—darkness.
*   **Corn with grains of all colors** on one ear represents the colors of the upper region—the sky <note>original: "firmament"</note>, with its rosy and yellow clouds and shining stars.
*   **“Speckled” corn**, where each grain contains all the colors, belongs to the “Priestess-Mother”—representing woman containing within herself the seeds of all races past, present, and future; similar to the concept of Eve being the mother of all living things.

Separate from these was the Sun—the Great Deity—whose priest was the spiritual head of the nation. These facts were confirmed by Mr. Frank Hamilton Cushing, who, as many know, became a member of the Zuñi tribe, lived with them, was initiated into their religious mysteries, and has learned more about them than any other man currently living.

<header>THE SECRET DOCTRINE.</header>

Seven is also the great magic number. In the Secret Records <note>original: "Occult Records"</note>, the weapon mentioned in the *Puranas* and the *Mahabharata*—the *Agneyastra* <note>original: *Âgneyâstra*</note> or “fiery weapon” given by the sage Aurva to his disciple <note>original: *Chelâ*</note> Sagara—is said to be constructed of seven elements. This weapon—which some clever scholars of Eastern cultures <note>original: "ingenious Orientalists"</note> have suggested was simply a “rocket” (!)—is one of the many frustrations for modern scholars of the Sanskrit language <note>original: "Sanskritists"</note>. Professor Wilson applies his keen intellect to this topic over several pages in his *Specimens of the Hindu Theatre*, and ultimately fails to explain it. He can make nothing of the *Agneyastra*, because he argues:

<margin>* See pp. 445, 446, above.</margin>
<margin>† Work cited <note>original: "Op. cit."</note>, i. 297, 2nd ed.</margin>
> These weapons are of a very mysterious character. Some of them are occasionally thrown as missiles; but, in general, they appear to be mystical powers exercised by the individual—such as those of paralyzing an enemy, or locking his senses fast in sleep, or bringing down storms, rain, and fire from heaven. . . . They are supposed to take on heavenly shapes, endowed with human abilities. . . . The *Ramayana* calls them the sons of Krishashva.†

<margin>‡ It is. But *Agneyastra* are fiery “missile weapons,” not “edged” weapons, as there is a difference between *Shastra* <note>hand-held weapons</note> and *Astra* <note>projectile weapons</note> in Sanskrit.</margin>
The *Shastra-devatas* <note>original: *Shastra-devatâs*</note>, or “Gods of the divine weapons,” are no more the *Agneyastras* <note>the weapons themselves</note> than modern artillery gunners are the cannons they direct. But this simple solution did not seem to occur to the eminent Sanskrit scholar. Nevertheless, as he himself says of the weapon-like descendants of Krishashva, “the symbolic <note>original: "allegorical"</note> origin of the [*Agneyastra*] weapons is, undoubtedly, the more ancient.”‡ It is the fiery javelin of Brahma <note>The Hindu creator god</note>.

The seven-part *Agneyastra*, like the seven senses and the seven human principles symbolized by the seven priests, is of incredibly ancient origin. The following section will show just how old the doctrine believed by Theosophists <note>Members of a philosophical movement seeking universal truth through ancient wisdom</note> really is.

Therefore, the causes and their effects worked in invisible or mystical Nature as well as in psychic Nature, and were related to Metaphysics and Psychology as much as to Physiology. Further on, the lecturer defines these seven (Egyptian) Souls as: (1) The Soul of Blood—the *formative* soul; (2) The Soul of Breath—the soul that *breathes*; (3) The Shade or Covering Soul—the soul that *envelopes*; (4) The Soul of Perception—the soul that *perceives*; (5) The Soul of Puberty <note>original: "Pubescence"</note>—the soul that *procreates*; (6) The Intellectual Soul—the soul that *reproduces intellectually*; and (7) The Spiritual Soul—the soul that is *permanently preserved*.

From a physical and external <note>original: "exoteric and physiological"</note> standpoint, this may be very correct; however, it is less accurate from the Esoteric <note>inner or hidden</note> point of view. To argue this does not mean at all that "Esoteric Buddhists" reduce *human beings into a collection of elementary spirits*, as Mr. Gerald Massey accuses them of doing in the same lecture. No "Esoteric Buddhist" has ever been guilty of such an absurdity. Nor has it ever been suggested that these shadows "become spiritual beings in another world," or "seven potential spirits or elementaries of another life." What is actually maintained is simply that every time the immortal **Self** <note>original: "Ego"</note> takes on a physical body, it becomes, as a whole, a compound unit of Matter and Spirit, which together act on seven different planes of existence and consciousness. Elsewhere, Mr. Gerald Massey adds:

> The seven souls [what we call "principles"] . . . are often mentioned in Egyptian texts. The seven stars in the hand of the Christ in the Book of Revelation have the same significance.‡

# THE "WATER-MEN" OF THE *BUNDAHISH*. <note>The *Bundahish* is an important Zoroastrian text concerning the creation of the world and cosmogony.</note>

God's powers, and the entire body of the world consists of the seven qualifying or fountain spirits.†

This is a rendering of our Theosophical doctrine into mystical language. However, how can we agree with Mr. Gerald Massey when he states that:

> The Seven Races of Men that have been refined <note>original: "sublimated"</note> and made Planetary [?] by Esoteric Buddhism,‡ may be found in the *Bundahish* as (1) the earth-men; (2) water-men; (3) breast-eared men; (4) breast-eyed men; (5) one-legged men; (6) bat-winged men; (7) men with tails.§

Each of these descriptions, though allegorical and even distorted in their later forms, is nonetheless an echo of the *Secret Doctrine* teaching. They all refer to the pre-human evolution of the "terrible and evil Water-men" created by Nature alone over millions of years, as previously described. But we flatly deny the assertion that "these were never real races," and we point to the *Archaic Stanzas* for our answer. It is easy to suggest and to say that our "instructors have mistaken these shadows of the Past for things human and spiritual"; but it is much harder to prove that "they are neither, and never were either." That assertion must always remain on a par with the Darwinian claim that humans and apes shared a common ape-like <note>original: "pithecoid"</note> ancestor. What the lecturer [Massey] treats merely as a "mode of expression" in the Egyptian Ritual, we view as having quite another and an important meaning. Here is one instance. The Ritual, known as the *Book of the Dead*, says:

> "I am the mouse." "I am the hawk." "I am the ape." . . . "I am the crocodile whose soul comes from MEN." . . . "I am the soul of the gods."||

The second to last sentence is explained by the lecturer, who adds parenthetically, "*that is, as a symbol of intelligence*," and the last as meaning, "the Horus, or Christ, as the final result of all."

->THE SECRET DOCTRINE.<-

The Occult Teaching answers: It means far more.

First of all, it confirms the teaching that while the human <term>Monad</term> <note>The eternal, divine spark or "true self" that evolves through many lifetimes.</note> passed through all three kingdoms—the mineral, the vegetable, and the animal—on Globe A and others during the First <term>Round</term> <note>In Theosophical cosmology, a "Round" is one of seven cycles of evolution that life passes through on a chain of planets.</note>, in this current Fourth Round, every mammal has actually descended from Man. This is true if we consider the semi-ethereal, multi-shaped creatures of the first two <term>Root Races</term>—which contained the human Monad—to be "Man." And they must be called such; for in <term>Esoteric language</term> <note>The specialized terminology used by initiates to describe hidden spiritual truths.</note>, "Man" is not the physical form of flesh, blood, and bones we see today, but rather the inner divine Monad with its many layers and aspects.

The lecture mentioned, however, despite its opposition to the book *Esoteric Buddhism* and its specific teachings, provides an eloquent response to those who try to portray these ideas as a brand-new invention. There are many such critics in Europe, America, and even India. Yet, the difference between the hidden knowledge of the ancient <term>Arhats</term> <note>Enlightened beings or advanced spiritual initiates in the Buddhist tradition.</note> and the philosophy preserved today by the few Brahmins in India who have seriously studied their Secret Philosophy does not appear very great. The difference seems mostly focused on and limited to the sequence of how cosmic and other principles evolved. At any rate, this disagreement is no greater than the eternal debate over the *filioque* <note>original: "filioque" — A Latin term meaning "and the Son," referring to a major theological dispute about the origin of the Holy Spirit that helped split the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.</note> dogma, which has separated the Roman Catholic Church from the older Greek Eastern Church since the eighth century. Nevertheless, regardless of the different ways the <term>sevenfold</term> <note>original: "septenary"</note> doctrine is presented, the core substance remains. Its presence and importance in the Brahmanical system can be seen in what one of India’s learned Vedantic scholars and metaphysicians says about it:

> The true hidden sevenfold classification is one of the most important, if not the most important, systems of organization, having been arranged according to the mysterious nature of this eternal archetype. I should also mention that the fourfold classification system claims the same origin. The light of life seems to be bent and split, as if by the three-sided prism of <term>Prakriti</term> <note>The fundamental substance or "Primal Nature" from which the physical universe is created.</note>—with the three <term>Gunas</term> <note>original: "Gunams" — The three fundamental qualities of nature: Sattva (purity/light), Rajas (passion/activity), and Tamas (inertia/darkness).</note> acting as its three faces—and divided into seven rays. Over time, these seven rays develop into the seven principles used in this classification. This development shows some similarities to the way the different colors of the light spectrum gradually appear. While a fourfold classification is more than enough for practical use, this true sevenfold system is of great theoretical and scientific importance. It is necessary to use it to explain certain types of phenomena noticed by occultists, and it is perhaps better suited to serve as the foundation for a perfect system of psychology. This is not the exclusive property of the "Trans-Himalayan Esoteric Doctrine." In fact, it has a closer connection with the Brah-

This School or Fraternity is closely connected with a certain island in an inland sea—believed in by both Hindus and Buddhists, but called "mythical" by geographers and <term>Orientalists</term> <note>Western scholars who study the languages and cultures of Asia.</note>—and the less one talks of it, the wiser he will be. # THE SECRET DOCTRINE.

However, there are very small differences between them—more imaginary than real, in fact. Brahmanism and Buddhism, when viewed from their orthodox perspectives, are as hostile and irreconcilable as water and oil. Each of these great systems, however, has a weak spot in its structure. While they might "agree to disagree" even in their hidden <term>esoteric</term> interpretations, once their respective weak points are confronted, every disagreement must vanish, for the two will find themselves on common ground. The "Achilles’ heel" <note>original: "Achilles’ heel"; a Greek idiom referring to a single vulnerable point in an otherwise strong person or system.</note> of orthodox Brahmanism is the <term>Advaita</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "Non-dualism"; a school of Hindu philosophy that teaches the oneness of the individual soul and the supreme reality.</note> philosophy, whose followers are called "Buddhists in disguise" by the pious. Likewise, the weak point of orthodox Buddhism is Northern Mysticism, represented by the disciples of the <term>Yogacharya</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "Teacher of Yoga"; a school of Buddhist philosophy emphasizing meditation and consciousness.</note> school of Aryasanga and the <term>Mahayana</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "Great Vehicle"; one of the two main branches of Buddhism.</note>. These Buddhists are mocked in turn by their fellow believers as "<term>Vedantins</term> <note>original Sanskrit: followers of the Vedanta, the concluding part of the Vedas.</note> in disguise." The hidden philosophy of both systems can only be one and the same if carefully analyzed and compared, as Gautama Buddha and Shankaracharya <note>The famous 8th-century philosopher who consolidated the Advaita Vedanta school.</note> are very closely connected, according to tradition and certain secret teachings. Thus, every difference between the two will be found to be a matter of form rather than of substance.

A highly mystical discourse, full of symbolism based on the number seven, can be found in the *Anugita*.* There, the <term>Brahmana</term> <note>A member of the highest Hindu caste, often a priest or teacher.</note> describes the bliss of having crossed beyond the regions of illusion:

> In which fancies are the gadflies and mosquitoes, in which grief and joy are cold and heat, in which delusion is the blinding darkness, in which greed is the beasts of prey and reptiles, and in which desire and anger are the ones who block the path.

The sage describes the entrance into and exit from the forest—a symbol for a person's lifetime—and also describes the forest itself:†

> In that forest are seven large trees [including the senses, the mind, and the understanding, or *Manas* <note>original Sanskrit: the "mind" or rational faculty.</note> and *Buddhi* <note>original Sanskrit: the "intellectual soul" or higher intuition.</note>], seven fruits, and seven guests; seven hermitages, seven forms of concentration, and seven forms of initiation. This is the description of the forest. That forest is filled with trees producing splendid flowers and fruits of five colors.

The senses, says the commentator:

> Are called trees, as they produce the fruits... of pleasures and pains...; the guests are the powers of each sense personified—they receive the fruits described above; the hermitages are the trees... in which the guests take shelter; the seven forms of concentration are the exclusion from the self of the—

-># AN ALLEGORY FROM THE "ANUGÎTÂ."<-

The seven functions of the seven senses, and so on, have already been mentioned. The seven forms of initiation refer to the initiation into the higher life by rejecting the actions of each member of the group of seven as not being one’s own.*

The following explanation is harmless, even if it is unsatisfactory. The <term>Brâhmana</term> <note>original Sanskrit: a member of the highest Hindu caste, often a priest or teacher.</note> continues his description:

> That forest is filled with trees producing flowers and fruits of four colors. That forest is filled with trees producing flowers and fruits of three colors, and mixed colors. That forest is filled with trees producing flowers and fruits of two colors, and of beautiful colors. That forest is filled with trees producing flowers and fruits of one color, and fragrant. That forest is filled [instead of with seven] with two large trees producing numerous flowers and fruits of indistinguishable colors [<term>mind</term> and <term>understanding</term>—the two higher senses, or theosophically, <term>Manas</term> and <term>Buddhi</term>]. There is one fire [the <term>Self</term>] here, connected with the <term>Brahman</term>,† and having a good mind [or *true knowledge*, according to the commentator Arjuna Mishra]. And there is fuel here (namely), the five senses [or *human passions*]. The seven forms of emancipation from them are the seven forms of initiation. The qualities are the fruits. . . . There . . . the great sages receive hospitality. And when they have been worshipped and have disappeared, another forest shines forth, in which *intelligence* is the tree, and emancipation is the fruit, and which possesses shade in the form of tranquillity; this forest depends on knowledge, has contentment for its water, and has the <term>Kshetrajñâ</term>‡ within acting as the sun.

Now, all of the above is very clear, and no Theosophist, even among those who are the least learned, can fail to understand the allegory. And yet, we see famous <term>Orientalists</term> <note>original: "Orientalists"; 19th-century Western scholars who studied the languages and cultures of Asia.</note> making a total mess of it in their explanations. The "great sages" who "receive hospitality" are explained as meaning the senses, "which, having worked as *unconnected with the self*, are finally absorbed into it." But it is hard to understand how the senses can be "absorbed into" the <term>Higher Self</term> if they are "unconnected" to it. One would think, on the contrary, that it is exactly because the *personal* senses gravitate toward and strive to be connected with the *impersonal* Self that the latter—which is Fire—burns away the lower five senses and thereby purifies the higher two: the "mind and understanding," or the higher aspects of <term>Manas</term>§ and <term>Buddhi</term>. This is quite obvious from the—

text. The “great sages” *disappear* after having “been worshipped.” Worshipped by whom, if they (the presumed senses) are “unconnected with the self”? By the Mind, of course; by <term>Manas</term> <note>original Sanskrit: the mind or processing faculty</note> (which in this case is merged with the *sixth sense*). This mind is not, and cannot be, the <term>Brahman</term> <note>the ultimate, impersonal reality or Absolute</note>, the Self, or the <term>Kshetrajña</term> <note>original Sanskrit: the "Knower of the Field," referring to the conscious Higher Self</note>—the Soul’s Spiritual Sun. In time, the Mind itself must be absorbed into that Higher Self. It has worshipped “great sages” and hosted *terrestrial wisdom*; but once “another forest shone forth” upon it, it is Intelligence (<term>Buddhi</term> <note>the faculty of spiritual intuition and discernment; the seventh sense or sixth principle in this system</note>) which is transformed into *the Tree*. This is the Tree whose fruit is emancipation (liberation), and which finally destroys the very roots of the <term>Ashvattha</term> <note>The sacred fig tree, used here as a symbol of the manifest universe and worldly life</note> tree—the symbol of *life* and its illusive joys and pleasures. Therefore, those who attain that state of liberation have, in the words of the sage quoted above, “no fear afterwards.” In this state, “the end cannot be perceived because it extends on all sides.”

“There always dwell seven females there,” the sage goes on to say, continuing the imagery. These females—who, according to the commentator Arjuna Mishra, are the <term>Mahat</term> <note>the Great Principle or Cosmic Mind</note>, <term>Ahamkâra</term> <note>the Ego-sense or "I-making" faculty</note>, and the five <term>Tanmâtras</term> <note>the subtle essences of the five senses</note>—always have their faces turned downwards, as they are obstacles in the way of spiritual ascension.

> In that same [Brahman, the Self] the seven perfect sages, together with their chiefs, . . . abide, and again emerge from the same. Glory, brilliance and greatness, enlightenment, victory, perfection and power—these seven rays follow after this same sun [the <term>Kshetrajña</term> or Higher Self]. . . . Those whose wishes are reduced [the unselfish]; . . . whose sins [passions] are burnt up by penance, merging the self in the self,* devote themselves to the Absolute. Those people who understand the forest of knowledge [Brahman, or the Self], praise tranquillity. And aspiring to that forest, they are [re-] born so as not to lose courage. Such, indeed, is this holy forest. . . . And understanding it, they [the sages] act accordingly, being directed by the Higher Self.

No translator among the Western Orientalists has yet perceived in this allegory anything higher than mysteries connected with sacrificial rituals, penance, ascetic ceremonies, or <term>Hatha Yoga</term> <note>a system of physical postures and breathing exercises</note>. But he who understands symbolic imagery, and hears the voice of *Self within Self*, will see in this something far higher than mere ritualism, however often he may err in the minor details of the Philosophy.

And here we must be allowed a final remark. No true Theosophist, from the most ignorant to the most learned, should claim to be infallible regarding anything he may say or write upon hidden (<term>Occult</term>) matters. The

<page-num>677</page-num>

<header>ENDLESS IS THE SEARCH FOR TRUTH.</header>

The main point is to admit that in many ways—whether classifying cosmic or human principles, outlining the order of evolution, or especially when dealing with metaphysical questions—those of us who attempt to teach others more ignorant than ourselves are all prone to making mistakes. Thus, errors have been made in *Isis Unveiled*, *Esoteric Buddhism*, *Man*, *Magic: White and Black*, and others; and more than one mistake is likely to be found in this current work as well. This is unavoidable. For a large or even a small work on such complex subjects to be completely free of error and blunders, it would have to be written from the first to the last page by a great <term>Adept</term> <note>a master of esoteric knowledge or a highly advanced spiritual being</note>, or even an <term>Avatara</term> <note>original Sanskrit: a divine incarnation or a being who has descended from a higher state to help humanity</note>. Only then could we say, “This is truly a work without sin or flaw!” But as long as the artist is imperfect, how can the work be perfect? “Endless is the search for truth!” Let us love it and strive for it for its own sake, and not for the glory or personal benefit that revealing even a tiny portion of it might bring us. For who among us can claim to have the *entire* truth at our fingertips, even regarding one minor teaching of Occultism?

However, our main goal in this current subject has been to show that the <term>septenary doctrine</term> <note>the teaching that the universe and humanity are composed of seven distinct layers or "principles"</note>—the division of the human constitution into seven parts—is very ancient and was not something we invented. This has been successfully demonstrated, for we are supported in this, both consciously and unconsciously, by a number of ancient, medieval, and modern writers. What the earlier writers said was phrased well; what more recent writers have repeated has generally been distorted. For example: read the *Pythagorean Fragments* and study the sevenfold nature of man as presented by Reverend G. Oliver, a learned Mason, in his book *The Pythagorean Triangle*, who speaks as follows:

> The Theosophic Philosophy . . . counted seven properties [or principles] in man—namely:
> (1) The divine golden man.
> (2) The inner holy body made of fire and light, like pure silver.
> (3) The elemental man.
> (4) The mercurial . . . paradisiacal man.
> (5) The martial, soul-like man.
> (6) The <term>venerine</term> <note>relating to the planet Venus; here associated with the ascending nature of desire</note>, ascending to outward desire.
> (7) The solar man, [a witness to and] an observer of the wonders of God [the Universe].
> 
> They also had seven "fountain spirits" or powers of nature.*

Compare this disorganized account and the way Western Theosophic Philosophy distributes these principles with the most recent Theosophic explanations by the—
